Diferent corticosteroids and regimens for accelerating fetal lung
maturation for babies at risk of preterm birth
Myfanwy J Williams1, Jenny A Ramson2, Fiona C Brownfoot3
1Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group, Department of Women's and Children's Health, University of Liverpool, Liverpool, UK.
2Sydney, Australia. 3Mercy Hospital for Women, Heidelberg, Australia
Contact: Fiona C Brownfoot, fiona.brownfoot@gmail.com.
Editorial group: Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group.
Publication status and date: New search for studies and content updated (no change to conclusions), published in Issue 8, 2022.
Citation: Williams MJ, Ramson JA, Brownfoot FC. Diferent corticosteroids and regimens for accelerating fetal lung
maturation for babies at risk of preterm birth. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 2022, Issue 8. Art. No.: CD006764. DOI:
10.1002/14651858.CD006764.pub4.
Copyright © 2022 The Cochrane Collaboration. Published by John Wiley & Sons, Ltd.
A B S T R A C T
Background
Despite the widespread use of antenatal corticosteroids to prevent respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) in preterm infants, there is currently
no consensus as to the type of corticosteroid to use, dose, frequency, timing of use or the route of administration.
Objectives
To assess the efects on fetal and neonatal morbidity and mortality, on maternal morbidity and mortality, and on the child and adult in
later life, of administering diferent types of corticosteroids (dexamethasone or betamethasone), or diferent corticosteroid dose regimens,
including timing, frequency and mode of administration.
Search methods
For this update, we searched Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register, ClinicalTrials.gov, the WHO International Clinical
Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP) (9 May 2022) and reference lists of retrieved studies.
Selection criteria
We included all identified published and unpublished randomised controlled trials or quasi-randomised controlled trials comparing any
two corticosteroids (dexamethasone or betamethasone or any other corticosteroid that can cross the placenta), comparing diferent dose
regimens (including frequency and timing of administration) in women at risk of preterm birth. We planned to exclude cross-over trials and
cluster-randomised trials. We planned to include studies published as abstracts only along with studies published as full-text manuscripts.
Data collection and analysis
At least two review authors independently assessed study eligibility, extracted data and assessed the risk of bias of included studies. Data
were checked for accuracy. We assessed the certainty of the evidence using GRADE.
Main results
We included 11 trials (2494 women and 2762 infants) in this update, all of which recruited women who were at increased risk of preterm
birth or had a medical indication for preterm birth. All trials were conducted in high-income countries.

Nine trials (2096 women and 2319 infants) compared dexamethasone versus betamethasone. All trials administered both drugs
intramuscularly, and the total dose in the course was consistent (22.8 mg or 24 mg), but the regimen varied. We assessed one new study
to have no serious risk of bias concerns for most outcomes, but other studies were at moderate (six trials) or high (two trials) risk of bias
due to selection, detection and attrition bias. Our GRADE assessments ranged between high- and low-certainty, with downgrades due to
risk of bias and imprecision.
Maternal outcomes
The only maternal primary outcome reported was chorioamnionitis (death and puerperal sepsis were not reported). Although the rate of
chorioamnionitis was lower with dexamethasone, we did not find conclusive evidence of a diference between the two drugs (risk ratio (RR)
0.71, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.48 to 1.06; 1 trial, 1346 women; moderate-certainty evidence). The proportion of women experiencing
maternal adverse efects of therapy was lower with dexamethasone; however, there was not conclusive evidence of a diference between
interventions (RR 0.63, 95% CI 0.35 to 1.13; 2 trials, 1705 women; moderate-certainty evidence).
Infant outcomes
We are unsure whether the choice of drug makes a diference to the risk of any known death afer randomisation, because the 95% CI was
compatible with both appreciable benefit and harm with dexamethasone (RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.63; 5 trials, 2105 infants; moderate-
certainty evidence). The choice of drug may make little or no diference to the risk of RDS (RR 1.06, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.22; 5 trials, 2105
infants; high-certainty evidence). While there may be little or no diference in the risk of intraventricular haemorrhage (IVH), there was
substantial unexplained statistical heterogeneity in this result (average (a) RR 0.71, 95% CI 0.28 to 1.81; 4 trials, 1902 infants; I2 = 62%; low-
certainty evidence). We found no evidence of a diference between the two drugs for chronic lung disease (RR 0.92, 95% CI 0.64 to 1.34;
1 trial, 1509 infants; moderate-certainty evidence), and we are unsure of the efects on necrotising enterocolitis, because there were few
events in the studies reporting this outcome (RR 5.08, 95% CI 0.25 to 105.15; 2 studies, 441 infants; low-certainty evidence).
Longer-term child outcomes
Only one trial consistently followed up children longer term, reporting  at two years' adjusted age. There is probably little or no diference
between dexamethasone and betamethasone in the risk of neurodevelopmental disability at follow-up (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.22; 2 trials,
1151 infants; moderate-certainty evidence). It is unclear whether the choice of drug makes a diference to the risk of visual impairment
(RR 0.33, 95% CI 0.01 to 8.15; 1 trial, 1227 children; low-certainty evidence). There may be little or no diference between the drugs for
hearing impairment (RR 1.16, 95% CI 0.63 to 2.16; 1 trial, 1227 children; moderate-certainty evidence), motor developmental delay (RR
0.89, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.20; 1 trial, 1166 children; moderate-certainty evidence) or intellectual impairment (RR 0.97, 95% CI 0.79 to 1.20; 1
trial, 1161 children; moderate-certainty evidence). However, the efect estimate for cerebral palsy is compatible with both an important
increase in risk with dexamethasone, and no diference between interventions (RR 2.50, 95% CI 0.97 to 6.39; 1 trial, 1223 children; low-
certainty evidence).
No trials followed the children beyond early childhood.
Comparisons of diferent preparations and regimens of corticosteroids
We found three studies that included a comparison of a diferent regimen or preparation of either dexamethasone or betamethasone
(oral dexamethasone 32 mg versus intramuscular dexamethasone 24 mg; betamethasone acetate plus phosphate versus betamethasone
phosphate; 12-hourly betamethasone versus 24-hourly betamethasone). The certainty of the evidence for the main outcomes from all
three studies was very low, due to  small sample size and  risk of bias. Therefore, we were limited in our ability to draw conclusions from
any of these studies.
Authors' conclusions
Overall, it remains unclear whether there are important diferences between dexamethasone and betamethasone, or between one regimen
and another.
Most trials compared dexamethasone versus betamethasone. While for most infant and early childhood outcomes there may be no
diference between these drugs, for several important outcomes for the mother, infant and child the evidence was inconclusive and did
not rule out significant benefits or harms.
The evidence on diferent antenatal corticosteroid regimens was sparse, and does not support the use of one particular corticosteroid
regimen over another.
P L A I N   L A N G U A G E   S U M M A R Y
Diferent corticosteroid treatments before early birth for improving outcomes for babies

Babies born early (before 37 weeks of pregnancy, which is considered preterm birth) are at increased risk of health problems. These
include lung problems (respiratory distress syndrome), bleeding of the brain (intraventricular haemorrhage) and death. Medicines called
corticosteroids are given to the mother while still pregnant to help stop these problems occurring and there is high-quality evidence that
they are efective in preventing many of these issues. These medicines work by maturing the baby's lungs before birth. There are diferent
types of corticosteroid and they can be given in diferent ways and in diferent doses. While we know that giving mothers at risk of early
birth corticosteroids has benefits for the baby, we do not know which type of corticosteroid is most beneficial and least harmful for mother
and baby.
Why is this important?
Since there is no clear or agreed best type or dose, hospitals may vary in how they give this medicine. This review assessed all available
evidence from randomised controlled trials (where the treatments people receive are decided at random; these trials usually give the most
reliable evidence about treatment efects) to determine which medicine and way of giving the medicine is best for mother and baby. We
 also wanted to find out what efect the medicines have once the babies have grown into children and adults.
What evidence did we find?
We searched for evidence on 9 May 2022, and identified 18 trials. We checked all trials for trustworthiness and did not include trials where
we had doubts. We included 11 trials (2494 women and 2762 babies). One of these trials included over 1500 babies, finished in 2013 and
was at low risk of bias. The other trials were smaller, older and at moderate or high risk of bias.
Nine trials compared the two corticosteroids most commonly used before early birth, dexamethasone and betamethasone. For the mother,
while there may be no diference between these medicines, we could not rule out the possibility that the risk of both infection and side
efects were lower with dexamethasone (moderate-quality evidence). For the baby, we are unsure whether the choice of medicine make
a diference to the risk of any death afer the start of the trial (moderate-quality evidence). The choice of medicine probably  makes
little or no diference to the risk of respiratory distress syndrome (high-quality evidence) and chronic lung disease (moderate-quality
evidence). We found that there may be little or no diference between dexamethasone and betamethasone in the risk of intraventricular
haemorrhage (low-quality evidence). We are uncertain whether the choice of medicine makes a diference to the risk of necrotising
enterocolitis (inflammation of the small and large intestines), because this happened so rarely in the trials (low-quality evidence).
One large trial attempted to monitor all children longer term, reporting results when children were two years of age. This trial found that
overall there is probably little or no diference in the risk of neurodevelopmental disability (illnesses that afect how the brain functions) at
two years of age (moderate-quality evidence). The choice of medicine may make little or no diference to specific developmental outcomes
including  hearing impairment (moderate-quality evidence), developmental delay (moderate-quality evidence) or learning dificulties
(moderate-quality evidence). It is unclear whether the choice of medicine makes a diference to sight impairment (low-quality evidence).
We are also unsure whether dexamethasone increases the risk of cerebral palsy (a group of disorders that afect the ability to move and
maintain balance and posture) because there were  few events in the one study looking at this. We need information from more children
to accurately assess the diferences between these medicines for this outcome (low-quality evidence).
Three trials compared diferent ways of giving corticosteroids. One trial compared two ways of giving dexamethasone (by mouth or
injection into the muscle), another trial compared diferent preparations of betamethasone and a third trial compared two ways of giving
betamethasone (diferent time intervals between doses). Because these trials were small and at moderate risk of bias, we do not know
whether their findings give a good indication of how best to give these medicines.
What does this mean?
Although we found that the efects of dexamethasone and betamethasone are probably similar for many outcomes, we are not sure which
is the best corticosteroid in the context of early birth. We found no trials that reported the efects of these medicines beyond two years of
age, so we cannot comment on their long-term efect on the child's health.
We did not find much evidence on the best way to give corticosteroids, so we are unable to say whether one way might be better than
another.
We need more studies to establish which is the best medicine and what is the best way to give it, and babies in these trials need to be
monitored over a long period to see any efects on child and adult development.

GRADE Working Group grades of evidence
High certainty: we are very confident that the true effect lies close to that of the estimate of the effect.
Moderate certainty: we are moderately confident in the effect estimate: the true effect is likely to be close to the estimate of the effect, but there is a possibility that it is
substantially different.
Low certainty: our confidence in the effect estimate is limited: the true effect may be substantially different from the estimate of the effect.

B A C K G R O U N D
Description of the condition
Preterm birth (less than 37 weeks' gestation) poses a significant
global health burden. National rates vary, and range from 5% to
19%, with over 80% of all preterm births occurring in south Asia
and sub-Saharan Africa (Chawanpaiboon 2019). Preterm infants,
especially those born before 32 weeks' gestation, are at high risk
of respiratory distress syndrome (RDS), a serious complication
that remains one of the most common causes of early neonatal
death and disability (Haram 2003; Patel 2016). Those infants born
preterm who do survive the neonatal period are at a significantly
increased risk of long-term neurological disability (Johnson 1993;
Mwaniki 2012; Saigal 2007). RDS develops as a consequence of
surfactant deficiency and immature lung development. The risk
of RDS and neonatal mortality reduces as gestation increases,
reflecting maturity of organ systems (Doyle 2001; Moise 1995; Saigal
2007). Treatments that may reduce the incidence of RDS in infants
born preterm, including antenatal corticosteroids, have therefore
received considerable attention. One recent Cochrane Review
that compared antenatal corticosteroid for fetal lung maturation
versus placebo concluded that the available evidence supports
the continued use of a single course of antenatal corticosteroids
(McGoldrick 2020).
Description of the intervention
Corticosteroid type
Currently either betamethasone or dexamethasone are the
recommended corticosteroids used in clinical practice (FIGO 2021).
Betamethasone is available in two forms: betamethasone sodium
phosphate, a solution with a short biological half-life of 36 to 72
hours; and betamethasone acetate, a suspension with a relatively
long half-life (Jobe 2004; Katzung 2004; NNF6 2011). These forms
of betamethasone are ofen used in combination to maximise the
drug's eficiency while reducing the number of injections given to
the mother (NNF6 2011). Dexamethasone generally comes in the
form of dexamethasone sodium phosphate (Ballard 1995; Jobe
2004; Katzung 2004; NNF6 2011).
Both betamethasone and dexamethasone can cross the placenta
in their active form and have comparable properties (NNF6 2011).
The chemical composition of betamethasone and dexamethasone
are virtually identical except for the configuration of a methyl group
in position 16 (Bar-Lev 2004; NNF6 2011). Some dexamethasone
preparations contain a sulphite preservative (NNF6 2011). Sulphites
have been linked to neurotoxicity in the newborn (Bar-Lev 2004;
Baud 1999; Goldenberg 2001; Walfisch 2001).
The optimal type of corticosteroid to use for antenatal treatment
remains unclear. The previous version of this review indicated
that it was uncertain whether one corticosteroid has advantages
over another (Brownfoot 2013). While the authors found that
dexamethasone may be associated with a reduced risk of
intraventricular haemorrhage (IVH) and a shorter stay in the
neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) when compared with
betamethasone, there were no diferences for other infant
outcomes, and none of the included studies reported any primary
or secondary maternal outcomes.
The long-term outcomes related to corticosteroid use have
largely been positive. The  McGoldrick 2020  Cochrane Review
concluded that overall, antenatal corticosteroid treatment was
probably associated with less developmental delay in childhood.
It is not known if the long-term outcomes vary by type of
corticosteroid used. While follow-up at 30 years following use
showed no clinical diferences in adults who were exposed or
not exposed to betamethasone in utero (Dalziel 2005), there
have been no similar long-term follow-up studies reported on
dexamethasone use. When this review was previously updated,
there were no published data on the long-term efects of antenatal
betamethasone compared directly with dexamethasone.
Corticosteroid dose, timing and frequency
The optimal corticosteroid dose to use, timing of use and frequency
of administration similarly remains unclear. The common regimens
of two doses of betamethasone 12 mg given intramuscularly
24 hours apart, and two doses of dexamethasone 12 mg given
intramuscularly 24 hours apart were recently recommended by the
International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO 2021),
although four doses of dexamethasone 6 mg given intramuscularly
12 hours apart has also been recommended (NIH 1995). This
total dose (24 mg) corresponds to a high occupancy of steroid
receptors in fetal tissues. While the benefits of corticosteroids are
well-known, there is concern regarding their potential for adverse
efects, particularly at high doses. There is a suggestion that the
current antenatal doses used may be higher than needed (Jobe
2021; Schmidt 2019). Similarly, the rationale for two doses of
betamethasone and either two or four doses of dexamethasone
and the efects of using diferent formulations for the initial and
subsequent injections remain unclear (Jobe 2004; NNF6 2011).
Corticosteroid route
The optimal route of administration of antenatal betamethasone
and dexamethasone is also uncertain. Both drugs may be
administered as intramuscular injections. Betamethasone can
be given intra-amniotically (Lefebvre 1976; Murphy 1982) and
intravenously (Petersen 1983), and dexamethasone can be given
orally (Egerman 1998).
Repeat doses of corticosteroid
The reduction in the incidence of RDS by antenatal corticosteroid
therapy is efective up to seven days afer treatment (McGoldrick
2020). One Cochrane Review assessed whether, for women who
remain undelivered and at risk of preterm birth, antenatal
corticosteroids need to be repeated seven days afer the initial
course (Crowther 2015); therefore, this review will not cover repeat
steroid courses compared with a single course.
How the intervention might work
Corticosteroids act by altering gene expression resulting in
glucocorticoid efects, including gluconeogenesis (synthesis
of glucose from non-carbohydrate metabolites); proteolysis
(breakdown of proteins); lipolysis (breakdown of lipids);
suppression of immune responses; and mineralocorticoid efects
(regulation of electrolyte excretion), including hypertension,
sodium and water retention, and potassium loss (AMH 2006).
In fetal lungs, the action of corticosteroids leads to an increase
in protein production, biosynthesis of phospholipids and the
appearance of surfactant (Ballard 1995).
Liggins 1969 demonstrated that the lungs of lambs born preterm
became functionally mature following antenatal corticosteroid

administration. Following these initial animal studies, Liggins and
other investigators conducted several clinical trials to assess the
efects of corticosteroids before preterm birth in humans.
The  McGoldrick 2020  Cochrane Review showed that a single
course of antenatal corticosteroids reduced the incidence of RDS,
perinatal death and neonatal death, and probably reduced IVH and
childhood developmental delay. For the mother, corticosteroid use
did not increase the risk of death, chorioamnionitis or endometritis
(McGoldrick 2020). Contrary to the concern that corticosteroid
treatment may increase infection in those with preterm prelabour
rupture of membranes (Imseis 1996), or increase the rate of
stillbirth in those with pregnancy-related hypertension (Liggins
1976), subgroup analyses in this Cochrane Review suggested that
antenatal corticosteroid treatment might not increase the risk
of these complications (McGoldrick 2020). Corticosteroids have
become the standard of care for women at risk of preterm birth
before 32 to 34 weeks' gestation in many countries (Jobe 2004; NIH
1995).
Despite their widespread use, there is currently variation in clinical
practice as to the type of corticosteroid used, the dose and
frequency given, and the route of administration of corticosteroid
doses.
Why it is important to do this review
Determining the optimal corticosteroid and optimal regimens is
very important since most pregnant women at risk of preterm
birth will be considered candidates for antenatal corticosteroid
treatment (NIH 2000), and these numbers may continue to grow as
rates of preterm birth are increasing in a number of countries (Chow
2013; Goldenberg 2007).
There is considerable variation reported between countries
as to whether health practitioners prefer dexamethasone or
betamethasone, with many likely reasons for these diferences
including availability and costs (dexamethasone is cheaper than
betamethasone so is widely used in low- and middle-income
countries) (Henderson-Smart 2007; Saengwaree 2005), impact of
inconsistent findings from observational studies (Baud 1999; Lee
2006), and influence of opinion leaders (Jobe 2004).
This review updates a previously published Cochrane Review on
diferent corticosteroids and regimens for accelerating fetal lung
maturation for women at risk of preterm birth (Brownfoot 2013).
That review found that dexamethasone may have some benefits
compared to betamethasone such as less IVH and a shorter length
of stay in NICU. Few other conclusions about optimal antenatal
corticosteroids or regimens could be made, and thus the review
concluded that high-quality evidence from randomised controlled
trials (RCT) on types of corticosteroids, dosage and other variations
in regimen was urgently needed in this area.
Despite the widespread use of antenatal corticosteroids to prevent
RDS in preterm infants, there is still no consensus as to the type of
corticosteroid to use, or the dose, frequency, timing of use or the
route of administration. We aimed to assess studies that compared
diferent regimens of corticosteroid type, dose, timing, frequency
of dose per treatment course and route of administration.
O B J E C T I V E S
To assess the efects on fetal and neonatal morbidity and
mortality, on maternal morbidity and mortality, and on the
child and adult in later life, of administering diferent types of
corticosteroids (dexamethasone or betamethasone), or diferent
corticosteroid dose regimens, including timing, frequency and
mode of administration.
M E T H O D S
Criteria for considering studies for this review
Types of studies
We included all identified published and unpublished RCTs or
quasi-RCTs comparing any two corticosteroids (dexamethasone
or betamethasone or any other corticosteroid that can cross the
placenta), comparing diferent dose regimens (including frequency
and timing of administration) in women at risk of preterm birth.
We excluded cross-over trials and cluster-randomised trials. We
included studies published as abstracts only along with studies
published as full-text manuscripts.
Types of participants
Women with a singleton or multiple pregnancy expected to give
birth preterm (before 37 weeks) as a result of spontaneous preterm
labour, preterm prelabour rupture of membranes or indicated
preterm birth.
Types of interventions
•
Diferent types of corticosteroids including dexamethasone,
betamethasone, hydrocortisone or any other corticosteroid that
can cross the placenta
•
Diferent corticosteroid regimens including dose, frequency,
timing and route of administration
We excluded trials that compared the efect of corticosteroids with
other interventions and trials assessing repeat corticosteroid doses
versus a single corticosteroid dose.
Types of outcome measures
These cover outcomes of maternal morbidity, perinatal morbidity
and mortality, child morbidity and mortality, child as adult
morbidity and mortality, and the use of health services by the

Search methods for identification of studies
The following methods section is based on a standard template
used by the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group.
Electronic searches
For this update, we searched Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth’s
Trials Register by contacting their Information Specialist (9 May
2022)
The Register is a database containing over 33,000 reports of
controlled trials in the field of pregnancy and childbirth. It
represents over 30 years of searching. For full current search
methods used to populate Pregnancy and Childbirth’s Trials
Register including the detailed search strategies for CENTRAL,
MEDLINE, Embase and CINAHL; the list of handsearched journals
and conference proceedings, and the list of journals reviewed
via the current awareness service, see pregnancy.cochrane.org/
pregnancy-and-childbirth-groups-trials-register.
Briefly, Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth’s Trials Register is
maintained by their Information Specialist and contains trials
identified from:
•
monthly searches of the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled
Trials (CENTRAL), which includes centralised searches of
ClinicalTrials.gov and the World Health Organization (WHO)
International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP);
•
weekly searches of MEDLINE (Ovid);
•
weekly searches of Embase (Ovid);
•
monthly searches of CINAHL (EBSCO);
•
handsearches of 30 journals and the proceedings of major
conferences;
•
weekly current awareness alerts for a further 44 journals plus
monthly BioMed Central email alerts.
These search results are screened and the full text of all relevant
trial reports identified through the searching activities described
above. Based on the intervention described, each trial report is
assigned a number that corresponds to a specific Pregnancy and
Childbirth review topic (or topics), and is then added to the Register.
The Information Specialist searched the Register for this review
using this topic number rather than keywords. This resulted in
a more specific search set that has been fully accounted for in
the relevant review sections (Included studies; Excluded studies;
Studies awaiting classification; Ongoing studies).
In addition, we searched ClinicalTrials.gov and the WHO ICTRP
(trialsearch.who.int/Default.aspx) for unpublished, planned and
ongoing trial reports on 9 May 2022 using the search methods
detailed in Appendix 1.
Searching other resources
We searched the reference lists of retrieved studies.
We did not apply any  language or date restrictions.

At least two review authors independently assessed all the

At least two review authors evaluated all studies against predefined

Assessment of risk of bias in included studies
Two review authors independently assessed risk of bias for each
study using the criteria outlined in the Cochrane Handbook for
Systematic Reviews of Interventions (Higgins 2011). We resolved any
disagreement by discussion or by involving a third author.
Note: one review author was also an author on the A*STEROID trial
(Crowther 2019). Two other review authors performed risk of bias
assessments for that trial.
1. Random sequence generation (checking for possible selection
bias)
We described for each included study the methods used to generate
the allocation sequence in suficient detail to allow an assessment
of whether it should produce comparable groups.
We assessed the methods as:
•
low risk of bias (any truly random process, e.g. random number
table; computer random number generator);
•
high risk of bias (any non-random process, e.g. odd or even date
of birth; hospital or clinic record number);
•
unclear risk of bias.
2. Allocation concealment (checking for possible selection bias)
We described for each included study the method used to conceal
the allocation sequence and determined whether intervention
allocation could have been foreseen in advance of, or during,
recruitment, or changed afer assignment.
We assessed the methods as:
•
low risk of bias (e.g. telephone or central randomisation;
consecutively numbered sealed opaque envelopes);
•
high risk of bias (open random allocation; unsealed or non-
opaque envelopes, alternation; date of birth);
•
unclear risk of bias.
3.1. Blinding of participants and personnel (checking for
possible performance bias)
We described for each included study, the methods, if any, used to
blind study participants and personnel from knowledge of which
intervention a participant received. We considered studies to be
at a low risk of bias if they were blinded, or if we judged that the
lack of blinding would be unlikely to afect results. We considered
studies be at high risk of bias if there was no blinding or incomplete
blinding, and the outcome was likely to be influenced by lack of
blinding. We considered studies to be at unclear risk if there was
insuficient information to permit a judgement of 'low risk' or 'high
risk'. We assessed blinding separately for diferent outcomes or
classes of outcomes.
We assessed the methods as:
•
low, high or unclear risk of bias for participants;
•
low, high or unclear risk of bias for personnel.
3.2. Blinding of outcome assessment (checking for possible
detection bias)
We described for each included study the methods used, if any, to
blind outcome assessors from knowledge of which intervention a
participant received. We considered studies to be at a low risk of
bias if they were blinded, or if we judged that the lack of blinding
would be unlikely to afect results. We considered studies be at
high risk of bias if there was no blinding or incomplete blinding,
and the outcome was likely to be influenced by lack of blinding.
We considered studies to be at unclear risk if there was insuficient
information to permit a judgement of 'low risk' or 'high risk'. We
assessed blinding separately for diferent outcomes or classes of
outcomes.
We assessed methods used to blind outcome assessment as:
•
low, high or unclear risk of bias.
4. Incomplete outcome data (checking for possible attrition bias
due to the amount, nature and handling of incomplete outcome
data)
We described for each included study and for each outcome or
class of outcomes the completeness of data including attrition
and exclusions from the analysis. We stated whether attrition and
exclusions were reported, the numbers included in the analysis
at each stage (compared with the total randomised participants),
reasons for attrition or exclusion where reported, and whether
missing data were balanced across groups or were related to
outcomes.  Where suficient information was reported or was
supplied by the trial authors, we included missing data in the
analyses which we undertook.
 We assessed the methods as:
•
low risk of bias (e.g. where there was no missing data or where
reasons for missing data were balanced across groups);
•
high risk of bias (e.g. numbers or reasons for missing
data imbalanced across groups; 'as treated' analysis done
with substantial departure of intervention received from that
assigned at randomisation);
•
unclear risk of bias.
5. Selective reporting bias (checking for reporting bias)
We described for each included study how the possibility of
selective outcome reporting bias was examined by us and what we
found.
We assessed the methods as:
•
low risk of bias (where it was clear that all of the study's
prespecified outcomes and all expected outcomes of interest to
the review had been reported);
•
high risk of bias (where not all the study's prespecified outcomes
had been reported; one or more reported primary outcomes
were not prespecified; outcomes of interest were reported
incompletely and so could not be used; study failed to include
results of a key outcome that would have been expected to have
been reported);

Measures of treatment efect
Dichotomous data
For dichotomous data, we presented results as risk ratio (RR) with
95% confidence intervals (CI).
Continuous data
For continuous data, we used the mean diference (MD) when
trials measured outcomes using the same method. If necessary,
we would have used the standardised mean diference to combine
trials that measured the same outcome, but used diferent
methods.
Unit of analysis issues
We considered cross-over trials and cluster-randomised trials
inappropriate for this research question.
The unit of randomisation was per woman: for maternal outcomes,
we used the number of women as the denominator; where
possible, for fetal and neonatal outcomes where some women
had multiple pregnancies,  we used the number of fetuses as the
denominator.
Dealing with missing data
In cases where trial data were missing, we first sought information
from the original trial investigators. Details of trial authors
contacted and the questions asked of them are contained in
the Characteristics of included studies table.
We recognise that some study outcomes may be applicable only
to a subset of participants, for instance morbidity outcomes can
only occur afer live birth. However, if the denominator is not based
on the intention-to-treat (ITT) principle (i.e. if it omits those who
died before birth), this could potentially bias the analysis, as the
comparison is then not between the randomised groups. Since we
could not be certain that predelivery fetal deaths were unrelated
to the intervention, we judged that the more appropriate method
would be to use numbers randomised as the denominator for all
our outcomes related to the fetus/neonate.
In the absence of appropriate statistical methods in the individual
trials to account for missing data, in the following situations we
deemed it appropriate to use the  denominator reported by the
trial rather than the number randomised in order to avoid making
  potentially misleading assumptions about the outcomes for those
women and fetuses with missing data:
•
where there was no explanation for women who were lost
to follow-up before giving birth and were not included in the
analysis of the individual trials;
•
where women were not included in trial analysis because they
were randomised in error (e.g. multiple pregnancy in a singleton
pregnancy-only trial);
•
where women or babies were not included in the trial analysis
for outcomes recorded postdischarge (e.g. developmental
outcomes at two years);
•
where continuous data were reported as mean and standard
deviation (as changing the total used to calculate these would
introduce errors).
Assessment of heterogeneity
We assessed statistical heterogeneity in each meta-analysis using
the Tau2, I2 and Chi2 statistics. We regarded heterogeneity as
substantial if the I2 statistic was greater than 30% and either the
Tau2 was greater than zero, or there was a low P value (less than
0.10) in the Chi2 test for heterogeneity.
Assessment of reporting biases
In future updates of this review, if there are 10 or more studies
in the meta-analysis, we will investigate reporting biases (such
as publication bias) using funnel plots. We will assess funnel
plot asymmetry visually. If asymmetry is suggested by a visual
assessment, we will perform exploratory analyses to investigate it.
Data synthesis
We carried out statistical analysis using the Review Manager 5
(RevMan 2011). We used fixed-efect meta-analysis for combining
data where it was reasonable to assume that studies were
estimating the same underlying treatment efect (i.e. where trials
were examining the same intervention, and the trials' populations
and methods were judged suficiently similar). Where there was
clinical heterogeneity suficient to expect that the underlying
treatment efects difered between trials, or where there was
substantial statistical heterogeneity, we used random-efects meta-
analysis to produce an overall summary if an average treatment
efect across trials was considered clinically meaningful. The
random-efects summary was treated as the average range of
possible treatment efects and we have discussed the clinical
implications of treatment efects difering between trials. If the
average treatment efect was not clinically meaningful, we would
not have combined trials.
Where we have used random-efects analyses, we have presented
the results as the average treatment efect with its 95% CI, and the
estimates of Tau2 and I2 statistic.

Subgroup analysis and investigation of heterogeneity
We performed separate comparisons for diferent types of
corticosteroids; and diferent preparations, timings and routes of
administration.
For comparison of dexamethasone versus betamethasone, the
dosing regimen varied between trials. To aid understanding of the
characteristics of the included studies, we presented the results
subgrouped by dosing regimen. We did not prespecify subgroup
analyses by dosing regimen, and, in any case, there were too few
trials in any one dosing regimen subgroup to support meaningful
subgroup analyses.
For the 2022 update, where data were available, we planned
to perform the following   subgroup analyses (for primary
outcomes only) because we believe that it is possible that these
characteristics may afect health outcomes with this intervention:
•
singleton versus multiple pregnancy;
•
preterm prelabour rupture of membranes at trial entry (yes or
no);
•
gestational age at trial entry (24 to 26 weeks, 27 to 29 weeks, 30
to 34 weeks, 35 to 37 weeks);
•
pregnancy-induced hypertension syndrome at trial entry (yes or
no);
•
chorioamnionitis at trial entry (yes or no; post hoc, i.e. not
prespecified in the protocol);
•
fetal growth restriction at trial entry (yes or no; post hoc, i.e. not
prespecified in the protocol);
•
pregestational and gestational diabetes at trial entry (yes or no;
post hoc, i.e. not prespecified in the protocol).
However, we were unable to undertake meaningful subgroup
analyses for these clinical characteristics. For all our primary
outcomes, only a maximum of five trials reported any of our
primary outcomes. Furthermore, all analyses were dominated by
results that could not be distinguished according to these clinical
characteristics, because for most trials the trial inclusion criteria
did not enable allocation to one or the other subgroup (most trials
would have been allocated to a mixed/unclear subgroup), or the
results were not presented stratified by the relevant covariate, or
both.
Where we identified substantial heterogeneity, we investigated it
using subgroup analyses and sensitivity analyses. We considered
whether an overall summary was meaningful, and, if it was, used
random-efects analysis to produce it.
We planned to assess subgroup diferences by interaction tests
available in Review Manager 5 (Review Manager 2020). We would
have reported the results of the subgroup analysis quoting the
Chi2statistic and P value, and the interaction test I2 value.
Sensitivity analysis
We planned sensitivity analyses to explore the efect of trial quality
assessed by concealment of allocation, by excluding studies with
clearly inadequate allocation of concealment, rated at 'high risk of
bias' for this component. However, only one quasi-randomised trial
was included in this version of the review and since no other trials
reported the same outcomes as this trial, a sensitivity analysis by
adequacy of allocation could not be carried out.

Eleven studies met our inclusion criteria and were assessed as
trustworthy for this update.
The previous update of the review included 12 studies. However,
two previously included studies are now awaiting classification
following reassessment and trustworthiness screening (Chen 2005
(TST); Danesh 2012 (TST)). As a result of the updated search,
we included one further study (Crowther 2019; consisting of nine
new reports and one report previously awaiting classification).
Our search also identified two new reports relating to previously
included studies, which we added to the other references for these
studies (Elimian 2007; Khandelwal 2012).
See Characteristics of included studies table for full details. All the
trials had full reports available (i.e. none were published as abstract
only), and all the data included in our analyses were from full
reports (Crowther 2019; Egerman 1998; Elimian 2007; Khandelwal
2012; Magee 1997; Mulder 1997; Mushkat 2001; Rotmensch 1999;
Senat 1998; Subtil 2003; Urban 2005).
Ten studies are now excluded.  In addition to eight studies
previously excluded from this review (Egerman 1997; Kurz
1993; Liu 2006; Romaguera 1997; Salzer 1982; Shanks 2010;
Vytiska-Binstorfer 1985; Whitt 1976), we excluded two further
trials:  IRCT2014090912789N6  (one new report) because the trial
was neither randomised nor quasi-randomised; and  Sukarna
2021 (two new reports) because the population did not meet our
inclusion criteria (included women up to 38 weeks' gestation).
See Characteristics of excluded studies table.
Nine studies are awaiting classification:  Romejko-Wolniewicz
2013 was awaiting classification in the previous update, pending
information requested from the trial authors; it was unclear
whether  Chhatrala 2015  (one report) was a randomised trial; as
stated above, two previously included studies did not meet all the
trustworthiness screening criteria (Chen 2005 (TST); Danesh 2012
(TST)), and five studies identified in the new search also did not
meet all the trustworthiness screening criteria (Gupta 2019 (TST);
Kashanian 2018 (TST); Rasool 2017 (TST); Tehrani 2014 (TST); Yahya
2021 (TST); nine new reports in total). We labelled all of the trials
that, based on our assessments, did not meet these criteria '(TST)'
for ease of reference. See  below and  Characteristics of studies
awaiting classification table.
Seven studies are ongoing (IRCT2015120415634N2; NCT01697098;
NCT04494529; NCT05114096; Schmitz 2019; TCTR20200729002;
WHO ACTION III; 12 reports). See  Characteristics of ongoing
studies table.
Screening eligible studies for trustworthiness
For this review update, we used the Cochrane Pregnancy
and Childbirth's Trustworthiness Screening Tool for the
first time (see  Selection of studies  for a description of
the tool; pregnancy.cochrane.org/news/identifying-and-handling-
potentially-untrustworthy-trials-pregnancy-and-childbirth-
cochrane). We identified six new studies that met our inclusion
criteria, in addition to 12 previously included studies. Of these 18
studies, we judged that seven did not meet the trustworthiness
screening criteria. These included two formerly included studies
(Chen 2005 (TST); Danesh 2012 (TST)), and five studies from the
updated search (Gupta 2019 (TST); Kashanian 2018 (TST); Rasool
2017 (TST); Tehrani 2014 (TST); Yahya 2021 (TST)).
•
We found no evidence of prospective registration for six studies
conducted since 2010 (Danesh 2012 (TST); Gupta 2019 (TST);
Kashanian 2018 (TST); Rasool 2017 (TST); Tehrani 2014 (TST);
Yahya 2021 (TST). We note that while trial registration records
were available for three of these studies, they were registered
during enrolment (Kashanian 2018 (TST); Tehrani 2014 (TST);
Yahya 2021 (TST)).
•
For all six  studies, we also sought to confirm the method of
randomisation: for five studies there were the same number
of women in each group but the method was not described
(Danesh 2012 (TST); Gupta 2019 (TST); Kashanian 2018 (TST);
Rasool 2017 (TST); Tehrani 2014 (TST)); and for one previously
included study, neither the method of randomisation nor the
number of women randomised to each group was reported (the
study included twin births and maternal outcomes) (Chen 2005
(TST)).
In all cases we attempted to contact the trial authors; some
authors replied but we considered that they did not provide
adequate information; some authors did not reply; or contact
details were unavailable (see  Characteristics of studies awaiting
classification table).

Included studies
We included 11 trials (2494 women and 2762 infants) in this update
(Crowther 2019; Egerman 1998; Elimian 2007; Khandelwal 2012;
Magee 1997; Mulder 1997; Mushkat 2001; Rotmensch 1999; Senat
1998; Subtil 2003; Urban 2005; see Characteristics of included
studies table).
Dates of the study, funding sources and declarations of interest
Dates of the studies
The included studies took place between 1994 and 2013,
although  Mulder 1997,  Mushkat 2001,  and  Urban 2005  did not
report the dates of the study.
Funding sources
The National Health and Medical Research Council, Australia
funded Crowther 2019. All the other studies did not report the
funding sources.
Declarations of interest
Crowther 2019, Elimian 2007, and Khandelwal 2012 declared that
the authors had no competing interests. All the other studies did
not report whether they had any conflicting interests.
Design
One trial was quasi-randomised (Mushkat 2001). The other studies
were RCTs.
Setting
All trials were conducted in hospital settings in high-income
countries. Three trials were conducted in the USA (Egerman
1998; Elimian 2007; Khandelwal 2012); two in France (Senat 1998;
Subtil 2003); two in Israel (Mushkat 2001; Rotmensch 1999); and
one in each of Australia and New Zealand (Crowther 2019), the
Netherlands (Mulder 1997), Poland (Urban 2005), and the UK
(Magee 1997).
Participants
All women were at increased risk of preterm birth or had a medical
indication for preterm birth. The gestational age at trial entry varied
between trials from 23 to 35 weeks of gestation.
Interventions
Dexamethasone versus betamethasone (comparison 1)
Nine 
trials 
compared 
intramuscular 
dexamethasone 
to
intramuscular betamethasone (2096 women and 2319 infants),
with new data for this update from one trial including 1346 women
and 1509 infants (Crowther 2019).
While the total dose in the course was consistently 22.8 mg or
24 mg of dexamethasone or betamethasone, the trials varied in
terms of preparation (corticosteroid salt), dose, dosing interval and
number of doses (for an overview of the interventions in each of the
dexamethasone and betamethasone groups, see Table 1):
•
dexamethasone phosphate 24 mg (6 mg, 12 hourly, 4
doses) versus betamethasone phosphate, acetate/phosphate or
dipropionate 24 mg (12 mg, 24 hourly, 2 doses) (total 517 women
and 577 infants; Elimian 2007; Rotmensch 1999; Subtil 2003;
Urban 2005);
•
dexamethasone (unspecified) 24 mg (12 mg, 12 hourly, 2 doses)
and betamethasone 24 mg (unspecified; or betamethasone
acetate/phosphate) (12 mg, 12 hourly, 2 doses) (total 91 women
and 91 infants; Magee 1997; Mushkat 2001);
•
dexamethasone phosphate 16 mg (4 mg, 12 hourly, 4 doses) and
betamethasone phosphate or acetate/phosphate 24 mg (6 mg,
12 hourly, 4 doses) (82 women and 82 infants; Senat 1998);
•
dexamethasone phosphate 24 mg (12 mg, 12 hourly, 2 doses)
and betamethasone acetate/phosphate 24 mg (12 mg, 24 hourly,
2 doses) (60 women and 60 infants; Mulder 1997);
•
dexamethasone phosphate 24 mg (12 mg, 24 hourly, 2 doses)
versus betamethasone acetate/phosphate 22.8 mg (11.4 mg, 24
hourly, 2 doses) (1346 women and 1509 infants; Crowther 2019).
Comparisons of diferent regimens and preparations of
dexamethasone or betamethasone (comparisons 2 to 4)
One trial compared diferent dexamethasone regimens: oral
dexamethasone phosphate 32 mg (8 mg, 12 hourly, 4 doses) versus
intramuscular dexamethasone phosphate 24 mg (6 mg, 12 hourly,
4 doses) (170 women and 183 infants; Egerman 1998).
The other two trials compared diferent preparations or regimens
(or both) of betamethasone. One three-arm trial compared two
forms of betamethasone (acetate plus phosphate versus phosphate
alone) (69 women and 69 infants; Subtil 2003).  This trial also
included a third group who received dexamethasone, which
we have included in the comparison of dexamethasone versus
betamethasone. The other trial compared dosing intervals of
betamethasone acetate plus phosphate (12 mg, 24 hourly, 2 doses
versus 12  mg, 12 hourly, 2 doses) (228 women and 260 infants)
(Khandelwal 2012).
Repeat courses
Five trials comparing dexamethasone versus betamethasone
allowed repeat weekly courses of the allocated corticosteroid
(Crowther 2019; Egerman 1998; Magee 1997; Mushkat 2001; Senat
1998) (see Table 1).
Primary outcomes in included studies
The primary outcomes varied between trials. The primary
outcomes of six trials focused on neonatal outcomes including

of neurodisability at 18 months (Subtil 2003)  or  24 months
(Crowther 2019). The other five trials concentrated on biophysical
parameters of the fetus (Magee 1997; Mulder 1997; Mushkat 2001;
Rotmensch 1999; Urban 2005).

For further details on the risk of bias in individual studies, see the
risk of bias table within the Characteristics of included studies
table.
Allocation
Methods of sequence generation and allocation concealment were
both adequate in five trials (low risk; Crowther 2019; Elimian 2007;
Khandelwal 2012; Magee 1997; Urban 2005).
In four further trials, while methods of random sequence
generation were adequate (low risk), methods to conceal allocation
were unclear (Egerman 1998; Rotmensch 1999; Senat 1998; Subtil
2003). One trial was at unclear risk of selection bias, with methods
of sequence generation and allocation concealment being unclear
(Mulder 1997).
In one trial, while the method of sequence generation was at low
risk of bias, participants were allocated alternately (based on odd/
even computer-generated number), so allocation concealment was
at high risk of bias (Mushkat 2001).
Blinding
Four trials were at a low risk of performance bias, with blinding
of women and personnel (Crowther 2019; Elimian 2007; Magee
1997; Mushkat 2001). For one trial, the risk of performance bias was
unclear, as blinding of women was not detailed (Rotmensch 1999).
The remaining six trials were at a high risk of performance bias, with
no blinding of women and study personnel (or blinding considered
unfeasible) (Egerman 1998; Khandelwal 2012; Mulder 1997; Senat
1998; Subtil 2003; Urban 2005).
Four trials were at a low risk of detection bias, with blinding of
outcome assessment (Crowther 2019; Elimian 2007; Khandelwal
2012; Magee 1997). One trial was at high risk of detection bias, with
no blinding of outcome assessors (Subtil 2003). The remaining six
trials were at unclear risk of detection bias (Egerman 1998;  Mulder
1997; Mushkat 2001; Rotmensch 1999; Senat 1998; Urban 2005).
Incomplete outcome data
Two trials were at low risk of attrition bias (Egerman 1998; Senat
1998).
While short-term loss to follow-up was minimal and well-
documented in Crowther 2019, there were losses of 20% to 25% in
both groups for longer-term outcomes, and, therefore, we assessed
this trial at unclear risk of attrition bias overall.
Two trials did not document losses to follow-up and were
at unclear risk of attrition bias (Mushkat 2001; Rotmensch
1999). Mulder 1997 reported a 17% loss to follow-up (6/30 from the
dexamethasone group and 4/30 from the betamethasone group),
and Elimian 2007 assessed less than 60% of all infants for IVH and
PVL. Urban 2005 did not mention exclusions or attrition; however,
all results were reported as a mean, and so it was not possible to
know whether there were losses. In Magee 1997 and Subtil 2003,
losses were greater than 50% at the end of follow-up for some of
the biophysical parameters.
Khandelwal 2012 was at high risk of attrition bias. In addition to
documented losses to follow-up for whom some outcomes are in
fact reported, the report states that only babies in whom clinical
evaluation was deemed relevant were assessed for some outcomes
(e.g. IVH, ROP, CLD); however, it was unclear whether all babies
were accounted for given inconsistent variation in denominators
for these outcomes.
Selective reporting
There was no obvious risk of selective reporting in two trials (low
risk; Crowther 2019; Subtil 2003).
While two trials prespecified their outcomes in the manuscript
methods, the risk of reporting bias was unclear, with outcome data
reported incompletely for some clinical outcomes (e.g. "gestational
age, birthweight and Apgar score at five minutes did not difer
between the two groups") (Egerman 1998; Mushkat 2001), or one
trial reported additional outcomes (Elimian 2007).
One trial reported all prespecified outcomes from the methods and
trial registration; however, the authors registered the trial during
recruitment and, therefore, we assessed risk of reporting bias as
unclear (Khandelwal 2012).
The remaining five trials reported some important clinical
outcomes; however, with no access to a trial protocol it was dificult
to confidently assess selective reporting; therefore, we judged
these studies at unclear risk of reporting bias (Magee 1997; Mulder
1997; Rotmensch 1999; Senat 1998; Urban 2005).
Other potential sources of bias
For nine trials, groups were comparable at baseline and there
were no other obvious sources of bias identified (Crowther 2019;
Egerman 1998; Elimian 2007; Magee 1997; Mulder 1997; Mushkat
2001; Rotmensch 1999; Subtil 2003; Urban 2005).
Two trials were at unclear risk of other bias; Khandelwal 2012 due
to some baseline imbalances between groups regarding age
and ethnicity, and  Senat 1998  because in the case of multiple
pregnancy, one fetus only was randomly selected for analysis.

1. Dexamethasone versus betamethasone
Nine trials including 2096 women and 2319 infants compared
dexamethasone versus betamethasone (Crowther 2019; Elimian
2007; Magee 1997; Mulder 1997; Mushkat 2001; Rotmensch 1999;
Senat 1998; Subtil 2003; Urban 2005).
Primary outcomes
Women
Chorioamnionitis
Although the rate of chorioamnionitis was lower with
dexamethasone when compared with betamethasone, given the
wide 95% CIs crossed the line of no efect, there was no conclusive
evidence of diference (RR 0.71, 95% CI 0.48 to 1.06; 1 trial, 1346
women;  anticipated absolute efects (AAE): 83 events per 1000
women with betamethasone, 24 fewer per 1000 women with
dexamethasone, 95% CI 43 fewer to 5 more; moderate-certainty
evidence; Analysis 1.1; Summary of findings 1).
Unreported outcomes
No studies reported maternal death or puerperal sepsis.
Fetus/neonate
Any known death afer randomisation
When combining the evidence on any known death afer
randomisation, there is probably no diference between
dexamethasone and betamethasone; however, given the wide 95%
CIs, the evidence is not conclusive (RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.63; 5
trials, 2105 infants; AAE 32 per 1000 infants with betamethasone,
1 more per 1000 infants with dexamethasone (95% CI 11 fewer to
20 more); moderate-certainty evidence; Analysis 1.2; Summary of
findings 2).
Respiratory distress syndrome
There is little or no diference in the risk of RDS between
dexamethasone and betamethasone (RR 1.06, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.22; 5
trials, 2105 infants; high-certainty evidence; Analysis 1.3; Summary
of findings 2).
Intraventricular haemorrhage
There was substantial statistical heterogeneity in the efect
estimate for IVH (average risk ratio (aRR) 0.71, 95% CI 0.28 to 1.81;
4 trials, 1902 infants; AAE 52 per 100 infants with betamethasone,
15 fewer with dexamethasone (38 fewer to 42 more); low-certainty
evidence; Analysis 1.4; Summary of findings 2; Tau2 = 0.38; Chi2 =
5.20, degrees of freedom (df) = 2 (P = 0.07); I2 = 62%). There were
too few trials contributing data to investigate this heterogeneity
with subgroup analyses as planned. However, one trial reported a
result that difered substantially from the other studies, suggesting
a substantial decrease in risk with dexamethasone (Elimian 2007).
We noted that this trial did not report on IVH for all infants (IVH
reported for 100/181 infants in dexamethasone group and 105/178
infants in betamethasone group), and sensitivity analysis removing
this study eliminated the statistical heterogeneity and suggests that
there may be little or no diference between drugs for this outcome
(RR 1.06, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.68; I2 = 0). The GRADE assessment (low)
reflects our lack of confidence in the pooled efect estimate, as well
as the wide 95% CIs.
Child
Death afer hospital discharge
One trial reported death afer hospital discharge, up to two years
adjusted age (Crowther 2019). There were few events in each group,
and the efect estimate had wide 95% CIs, so  we are uncertain
whether the choice of dexamethasone versus betamethasone
makes a diference to the risk of this outcome (RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.11
to 3.89; 1 trial, 1509 infants; Analysis 1.5).
Neurodevelopmental disability at follow-up
Two trials followed up children into childhood, however only one
of them attempted to follow up all surviving infants (Crowther
2019). The results suggest that there is probably little or no
diference between dexamethasone and betamethasone in the risk
of neurodevelopmental disability at follow-up (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.85
to 1.22; 2 trials, 1151 infants; moderate-certainty evidence; Analysis
1.6; Summary of findings 3). Crowther 2019 followed up children to
two years' adjusted age (with balanced loss to follow-up 22% with
dexamethasone versus 26% with betamethasone), and children
were considered to have a neurodevelopmental disability if they
had cerebral palsy, were blind or deaf, or showed developmental
delay (defined as a Bayley Infant and Toddler Development Scale,
version 3 (BSID-III) score in any of the cognitive, language and
motor domains of greater than one standard deviation below the
mean). Subtil 2003  followed up a subgroup of 12 children (eight
in dexamethasone group versus four in betamethasone group) to
18 months (adjustment not mentioned), all of whom had been
admitted to NICU as babies, and contributed only 0.4% to the
weight of the pooled efect estimate.
Child as an adult
The longest that any of the included trials followed up children
was to two years of age (adjusted for prematurity), therefore, no
studies reported primary outcomes for the child as an adult (death
or neurodevelopmental disability at follow-up).
Secondary outcomes
Women
Fever afer trial entry requiring the use of antibiotics
For the mother, there is probably  little or no diference between
dexamethasone and betamethasone in the risk of postnatal fever
requiring the use of antibiotics (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.23; 1 trial,
1346 women; Analysis 1.7).
Adverse efects of therapy
The rate of maternal adverse efects of therapy was lower with
dexamethasone; however, there was no conclusive evidence of
a diference between interventions given the 95% CIs  (RR 0.63,
95% CI 0.35 to 1.13; 2 trials, 1705 women; AAE 33 events per
1000 women with betamethasone, 12 fewer per 1000 women with
dexamethasone (95% CI 22 fewer to 4 more); moderate-certainty
evidence; Analysis 1.8; Summary of findings 1).
Unreported outcomes
No studies reported intrapartum fever requiring the use of
antibiotics, postnatal fever requiring the use of antibiotics,
admission to intensive care unit, glucose intolerance or
hypertension.

Fetus/neonate
Fetal death
There may be little or no diference between dexamethasone and
betamethasone in the risk of fetal death (RR 1.19, 95% CI 0.50 to
2.87; 1 trial, 1509 infants; Analysis 1.9).
Neonatal death
There may be little or no diference between dexamethasone and
betamethasone in the risk of neonatal death (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.58
to 1.80; 5 trials, 2105 infants; Analysis 1.10). One neonate died four
days afer birth (Mulder 1997), one neonate with severe intrauterine
growth restriction (IUGR) died one day afer caesarean section at 27
weeks' gestation (Subtil 2003), and in the other trials contributing
data, there was no further information about timing.
Apgar score less than 7 at five minutes
Only one small study reported Apgar score less than 7 at five
minutes, and we are uncertain whether there is a diference
between dexamethasone and betamethasone given the low
number of babies, few events and very wide 95% CIs (RR 0.54, 95%
CI 0.05 to  5.60; 1 trial, 50 infants; Analysis 1.11).
Birthweight
The choice of corticosteroid may make no diference to mean
birthweight (MD 0.03 kg, 95% CI –0.05 to 0.11; 5 trials, 2066
infants; Analysis 1.12).
Low birthweight
The choice of corticosteroid may make no diference to whether the
baby is at risk of being of low birthweight (RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.65 to
1.24; 1 trial, 105 infants; Analysis 1.13).
Mean length at birth
There may be little diference in the mean length at birth
between groups (MD 0.10 cm, 95% CI –0.47 to 0.67; 1 trial, 1489
infants; Analysis 1.14).
Mean head circumference at birth
There may be little diference in the mean head circumference at
birth between groups (MD 0.20 cm, 95% CI –0.18 to 0.58; 1 trial, 1489
infants; Analysis 1.15).
Admission to neonatal intensive care
There was substantial statistical heterogeneity in the efect
estimate for admission to NICU (aRR 1.75, 95% CI 0.49 to 6.25; 2
trials, 1614 infants; Analysis 1.16; Tau2 = 0.71; Chi2 = 5.18, df = 1
(P = 0.02); I2 = 81%). Only two studies contributed data, with one
small study reporting few events but twice as many in the smaller
dexamethasone group (8/36 in the dexamethasone group versus
4/69 in the betamethasone group) (Subtil 2003). It was not possible
to investigate this heterogeneity with subgroup analyses given that
only two trials contributed data. It is possible that diferences in the
reasons for preterm birth, or other clinical factors, contributed to
this heterogeneity. Sensitivity analysis limited to Crowther 2019, a
large multicentre study free of significant risk of bias concerns, gave
an efect estimate RR of 1.02 (95% CI 0.89 to 1.17), suggesting that
the choice of drug may make little or no diference to this outcome.
Need for mechanical ventilation
There is probably little or no diference between dexamethasone
and betamethasone in the need for mechanical ventilation  (RR
0.94, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.19; 1 trial, 1509 infants; Analysis 1.17).
Mean duration of mechanical ventilation
There is probably little or no diference between dexamethasone
and betamethasone in the mean duration of mechanical ventilation
(MD –0.38 days, 95% CI –1.11 to 0.35; 1 trial, 1509 infants; Analysis
1.18).
Severity of respiratory distress syndrome
There is probably no diference between dexamethasone and
betamethasone for the risk of moderate/severe RDS (RR 1.06, 95%
CI 0.80 to 1.39; 1 trial, 1509 infants; Analysis 1.19).
Chronic lung disease
There is probably no diference between dexamethasone and
betamethasone for the risk of chronic lung disease (RR 0.92,
95% CI 0.64 to 1.34; 1 trial, 1509 infants; moderate-certainty
evidence; Analysis 1.20; Summary of findings 2).
Bronchopulmonary dysplasia
There was substantial statistical heterogeneity in the analyses
for bronchopulmonary dysplasia (aRR 2.50, 95% CI 0.10 to
61.34; 2 trials, 464 infants;  Analysis 1.21); there was no clear
explanation for the heterogeneity (Tau2 = 4.40; Chi2 = 4.89,
df = 1 (P = 0.03); I2 = 80%).  Elimian 2007  reported 18/178
events in the dexamethasone group versus 27/181 events in
the betamethasone group, while  Subtil 2003  reported 4/36
events in the dexamethasone group versus 0/69 events in the
betamethasone group; for some other outcomes (e.g. admission to
NICU; Analysis 1.16), Subtil 2003 difered from other trials in the
high number of negative events for babies in the dexamethasone
group. It is possible that limitations in the study design (risk of bias),
diferences in reasons for preterm birth or other clinical factors
might explain this diference.

There were no clear diferences between dexamethasone and
betamethasone for the risk of severe IVH (RR 0.40, 95% CI 0.14 to
1.13; 4 trials, 1901 infants; Analysis 1.22).

There were no clear diferences between dexamethasone and
betamethasone for the risk of periventricular leukomalacia (RR
0.64, 95% CI 0.18 to 2.25; 4 trials, 1901 infants; Analysis 1.23).

There were no clear diferences between dexamethasone and
betamethasone for the risk of neonatal sepsis (RR 1.14, 95% CI 0.60
to 2.17; 1 trial, 359 infants; Analysis 1.24).

There were no clear diferences between dexamethasone and
betamethasone for the risk of necrotising enterocolitis (RR 5.08,
95% CI 0.25 to 105.15; 2 studies, 441 infants; low-certainty
evidence; Analysis 1.26).

dexamethasone group versus 8/746 events in the betamethasone
group; Elimian 2007 reported 26/178 events in the dexamethasone
group versus 28/181 events in the betamethasone group), and we
are not confident that the point estimate reflects the true diference
between dexamethasone and betamethasone.

Biophysical parameters
Six trials reported a range of biophysical parameters for a small
numbers of babies  (Crowther 2019; Magee 1997; Mushkat 2001;
Rotmensch 1999; Senat 1998; Subtil 2003).
In five trials there were some diferences in biophysical parameters
relating to fetal heart rate, fetal movements and fetal breathing
(Magee 1997; Mushkat 2001; Rotmensch 1999; Senat 1998; Subtil
2003):
•
the dexamethasone group had a lower fetal heart rate than
the betamethasone group at day two in Rotmensch 1999 (MD
–4.20 beats per minute, 95% CI –7.17 to –1.23; 1 trial, 46
infants; Analysis 1.29) and in Senat 1998 (Analysis 1.30), but not
in Magee 1997;
•
the dexamethasone group had a higher level of fetal movements
detected via ultrasound than the betamethasone group (MD
7.0 movements per hour, 95% CI 2.15 to 11.85; 1 trial, 33
infants; Mushkat 2001; Analysis 1.34);
•
at day two, the dexamethasone group had a higher breathing
times than the betamethasone group (MD 32.00 seconds in 30
minutes, 95% CI 4.37 to 59.63; 1 trial, 46 infants;  Rotmensch
1999; Analysis 1.37).
However,  Crowther 2019  found no diferences between groups
for any biophysical measures.  Crowther 2019  reported on a
small substudy involving 43/1346 women (47/1509 fetuses)
from two study centres, for whom the clinical team felt
delaying corticosteroids for pretreatment ultrasound would not
compromise clinical care, there was no suspicion of abnormal fetal
cardiac morphology and who were not taking medication with
potential major fetal cardiovascular efect. This substudy reported
on short-term ultrasound and cardiotocography (CTG) efects of
dexamethasone versus betamethasone, up to seven to 10 days afer
administration. The authors concluded that there was no evidence
of a diference between dexamethasone and betamethasone for
fetal or maternal Doppler studies, biophysical profile or CTG.
The other five trials also found no clear diferences between
betamethasone and dexamethasone for other biophysical
parameters including:
•
accelerations per hour (MD 2.80, 95% CI –0.15 to 5.75; 1 trial, 46
infants; Rotmensch 1999; Analysis 1.31);
•
fetal movements in 30 minutes (MD 2.30, 95% CI –0.74 to 5.34; 1
trial, 46 infants; Rotmensch 1999; Analysis 1.32);
•
fetal movement via maternal perception (MD 3.00 movements
per hour, 95% CI –3.20 to 9.20; 1 trial, 33 infants; Mushkat 2001;
Analysis 1.33); and
•
fetal breathing movements per hour (MD 0, 95% CI –2.05 to 2.05;
1 trial, 33 infants; Mushkat 2001; Analysis 1.36).
Subtil 2003  measured a range of fetal heart rate indicators but
only reported them in graphical form; the trial authors reported
that none of the indicators showed significant diferences between
dexamethasone and betamethasone.

D I S C U S S I O N
Summary of main results
This update includes 11 trials (2494 women and 2762 infants).
We implemented the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth's
Trustworthiness Screening Tool for the first time, removing data
from two previously included trials as a result (Chen 2005 (TST);
Danesh 2012 (TST)), and adding one large new trial (the A*STEROID
trial, Crowther 2019), adding 937 women and 1101 infants overall
since the previous update. For the comparison of dexamethasone
versus betamethasone, this afected most previously included
outcomes while adding information on some maternal outcomes
and longer-term outcomes for the child. There was no new evidence
on any other comparisons.
Dexamethasone versus betamethasone
Nine trials including 2096 women and 2319 infants compared
dexamethasone versus betamethasone, and while the route
(intramuscular) and total dose in the course given was consistent,
the dose, number of doses, dosing interval and drug preparation
varied (see Table 1). While we did not identify clear evidence of
a diference between the two drugs, there is some uncertainty
around potential important diferences for several maternal, infant

of a diference between the two drugs for chorioamnionitis.
Although the point estimate suggested a risk reduction with
dexamethasone, the 95% CIs included one (moderate-certainty
evidence). No included studies reported our other primary
outcomes for the mother (death and puerperal sepsis). In terms
of our main secondary outcomes, the rate of maternal adverse
efects was lower with dexamethasone, but again we did not
find conclusive evidence that there is a true diference between
drugs (moderate-certainty evidence). The only other secondary
outcome  reported for the mother was postnatal fever requiring
antibiotics, and the choice of drug probably makes little or no
diference to the risk of this outcome.
For primary outcomes for the baby, the point estimate suggests that
the choice of drug probably makes little or no diference to the risk
of any death afer randomisation; however, the 95% CI included
the possibility for both appreciable benefit and appreciable harm
with dexamethasone (moderate-certainty evidence), while there
is probably little or no diference to the risk of RDS (high-
certainty evidence). There may be little or no diference between
dexamethasone and betamethasone in the risk of IVH; however,
there was substantial unexplained statistical heterogeneity in the
efect estimate. In terms of our main secondary outcomes for the
baby, there may little or no diference between dexamethasone
and betamethasone for chronic lung disease, but the analysis
for necrotising enterocolitis was underpowered to identify any
diferences. For other secondary outcomes, analyses for some less
common neonatal morbidity outcomes were underpowered to
detect the true efect (e.g. Apgar score less than 7 at five minutes,
bronchopulmonary dysplasia, neonatal sepsis, neonatal infection
in the first 48 hours, severe IVH, retinopathy of prematurity), and
there was also substantial unexplained statistical heterogeneity
in the efect estimates for some   neonatal morbidity outcomes
(bronchopulmonary dysplasia, retinopathy of prematurity).
Although extensively reported in several of the older included
trials (Magee 1997; Mushkat 2001  Rotmensch 1999; Senat 1998;
Subtil 2003), and also included in a small substudy of  Crowther
2019, the clinical significance of any diferences in biophysical
parameters such as fetal heart rate and respiratory rate was
not clear (Rotmensch 1999). Crowther 2019 found no diferences
between groups for any biophysical parameters, fetal or maternal
Doppler studies, or CTG, although we note that this substudy
included only a small subset of the total women randomised
(and is accordingly described by the authors as a prospective
cohort study). Some of the older trials found indications of a lower
heart rate at day two, a longer duration of breathing time at day
two, and more fetal movements detected via ultrasound for the
dexamethasone group. Some authors suggest that the influence of
antenatal corticosteroids on parameters such as fetal heart rate is
not clinically important, being a transient physiological response
(Magee 1997; Rotmensch 1999; Subtil 2003).
Only one study attempted to follow up all children longer term,
at two years of age adjusted for prematurity, and this study
overwhelmingly drove the findings that there is probably little or
no diference between dexamethasone and betamethasone in the
risk of neurodevelopmental disability. The findings from this study
found no clear diferences to our other main longer-term outcomes
(visual impairment, hearing impairment, motor developmental
delay, intellectual impairment), or to other secondary outcomes
at the same time point (mean weight, height, head circumference,
systolic or diastolic blood pressure, or most other developmental
outcomes). However, the efect estimate for cerebral palsy
is compatible with both an important increase in risk with
dexamethasone, and no diference between interventions for this
outcome (low-certainty evidence).
Comparisons of diferent regimens and preparations of
dexamethasone or betamethasone
We found three studies that each included a comparison of
a diferent regimen or preparation of either dexamethasone
or betamethasone (dexamethasone 32 mg orally versus
dexamethasone 24 mg intramuscularly; betamethasone acetate
plus phosphate versus betamethasone phosphate; 12-hourly
betamethasone versus 24-hourly betamethasone). While it is
noteworthy that the first of these studies was stopped early due to
safety concerns relating to oral dexamethasone, we were limited
in our ability to draw conclusions from any of these studies due
to their small sample size, concerns about risk of bias and limited
number of outcomes reported.
Overall completeness and applicability of evidence
All trials were conducted in high-income countries, which may limit
the wider applicability of this review's findings.
The gestational age at trial entry varied from 23 to 35 weeks
of gestation. While women in all trials were at increased risk
of preterm birth or had a medical indication for preterm birth,
assessment of risk was not described in a number of studies.
For comparison of dexamethasone versus betamethasone, the
included studies did not report most of our outcomes for the
mother, so it is impossible to provide a complete picture of the
efect of choice of drug on the woman's health and well-being.
There are important uncertainties around some severe neonatal
morbidities and one longer-term developmental outcome
(including some outcomes that we judged to be most important,
namely IVH, necrotising enterocolitis and cerebral palsy), in large
part due to rarity and associated imprecision or heterogeneity
between trials, or both. Our analyses were further limited as not all
studies reported these neonatal outcomes. Assessment of longer-
term outcomes is crucial to any review of the efectiveness and
safety of antenatal corticosteroids for women and babies. Only one
study attempted to follow up all infants longer term, but there was
attrition at two-year follow-up. No studies provided data on longer-
term follow-up.
Most of the data available focused on the type of corticosteroid
used, with nine studies comparing the two most commonly used
corticosteroids, dexamethasone and betamethasone (with some
variation in frequency and timing of administration). Considering
the full scope of this review, our ability to reach comprehensive
conclusions was limited by the small number of comparisons
of diferent antenatal corticosteroid regimens. Evidence about
optimal doses, timing, frequency of administration and preparation
of specific antenatal corticosteroids was sparse, with three small
trials contributing data to three separate comparisons.
