Quality of the evidence
We included 11 trials (involving 2494 women and 2762 infants) in
this review update, including one large trial that was at minimal
risk of bias overall (Crowther 2019), eight trials that we found to be
at moderate risk of bias, and two further trials that we deemed to
be at more serious risk of bias (Mulder 1997; Mushkat 2001). Our
most common risk of bias concerns related to a lack of blinding of
participants and personnel, missing outcome data and uncertainty
about selective reporting bias. More serious worries related to
selection bias (in Mulder 1997 the method of sequence generation
was unclear, and Mushkat 2001 was quasi-randomised).
Our GRADE assessments factored in these risk of bias concerns, as
well as downgrades for imprecision, due to small sample size, few
events or wide CIs.
Potential biases in the review process
One review authors was also an author on the A*STEROID
trial (Crowther 2019). Two other review authors performed data
extraction and risk of bias assessments for that trial.
To improve the reliability of the results reported in this review,
and in line with current Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth group
policy, we implemented the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth's
Trustworthiness Screening Tool for the first time in this review.
We acknowledge that while the process involved was rigorous and
systematic, it also involved a degree of subjective judgement, and it
is possible that a diferent author team would have made diferent
decisions about inclusion of studies and data. In this respect, the
TST is similar to the assessment of risk of bias or the GRADE
process; in all cases, we sought to be consistent and transparent,
and thoroughly document our decisions and underlying rationale.
Agreements and disagreements with other studies or
reviews
One Cochrane Review comparing antenatal corticosteroids for fetal
lung maturation versus placebo conducted subgroup analyses by
type of corticosteroid therapy (McGoldrick 2020). While for most
outcomes these analyses did not support the hypothesis that there
is a diference between drugs, there may be some indication of a
diference between dexamethasone and betamethasone for RDS,
moderate/severe RDS and chorioamnionitis. For chorioamnionitis,
the subgroup analyses suggested that the risk may be reduced with
betamethasone but may be increased with dexamethasone, while
conversely our results suggest there may be a reduction in risk
with dexamethasone. However, for all three outcomes, the authors
noted the observed diferences may be due to chance.
One recent systematic review and network meta-analysis
specifically investigated dexamethasone versus betamethasone
for preterm birth (Ciapponi 2021). The authors concluded
that their review identified no important diferences between
dexamethasone and betamethasone for most key neonatal and
neurodevelopmental outcomes; however, they observed that there
may be clinically important diferences between these drugs for
chorioamnionitis, fetal death, endometritis or puerperal sepsis,
and RDS. Due to these uncertainties, which do not consistently
align towards one drug or the other, the authors argued that
further research is warranted. Although our review did not identify
the same concerns relating to fetal death or RDS, we also found
important uncertainties around some critical outcomes, with
inconclusive evidence that may favour either dexamethasone
(for chorioamnionitis, maternal adverse efects of therapy) or
betamethasone (for cerebral palsy), and missing evidence on key
outcomes including puerperal sepsis.
One recent review article raised concerns about the use of
betamethasone acetate in antenatal corticosteroid therapy, and
the size of the dose of antenatal corticosteroid (dexamethasone
or betamethasone) that women receive (Jobe 2021). We found
the evidence was inadequate to further understanding of
these concerns. Most studies included in our review that
compared dexamethasone versus betamethasone administered a
betamethasone preparation that included betamethasone acetate,
and all women in both groups received a similar total dose (22.8
mg to 24 mg). We only found one small three-arm study that
included a comparison of diferent betamethasone preparations
(betamethasone acetate plus phosphate versus betamethasone
phosphate), but it provided only very low-certainty evidence for all
reported outcomes (Subtil 2003).
A U T H O R S '   C O N C L U S I O N S
Implications for practice
We found no clear diferences between dexamethasone and
betamethasone. For some important outcomes for the woman
(chorioamnionitis and adverse efects of therapy),  it is possible
that dexamethasone may have some benefits over betamethasone,
but the evidence was not conclusive, and evidence was missing
on other key outcomes. In terms of outcomes for the baby
and child, there may be no diference between dexamethasone
and betamethasone for many outcomes; however, there are
uncertainties for some important neonatal outcomes (IVH,
necrotising enterocolitis) that do not rule out diferences, and
one early childhood outcome (cerebral palsy) does not rule out
harm with dexamethasone. We do not know about the longer-term
impact of these medications for the older child or into adulthood.
We found insuficient evidence to support the use of one particular
corticosteroid regimen over another.
Implications for research
For the comparison of dexamethasone and betamethasone, while
this review includes important evidence from one recent large
study, there remain some important uncertainties about the
relative benefits and harms of these two drugs, which may warrant
further research. We note that unresolved questions regarding the
drug regimen are also relevant to any trials that compare one type
of corticosteroid with another.
Our search identified one trial that is investigating the safety and
eficacy of antenatal corticosteroids in the late pre-term period (34
weeks 0 days to 36 weeks 6 days' gestational age) in low-income
countries (WHO ACTION III). The trial is aiming to recruit 13,500
women across five countries. All countries include the same three-
arm comparison of a standard dose and regimen of dexamethasone
(4 × 6 mg, 12-hourly), with a lower dose betamethasone phosphate
regimen (4 × 2 mg, 12-hourly), and similar placebo.
We found sparse evidence on diferent antenatal corticosteroid
regimens (route, drug preparation, total dose in course, dose,
number of doses, dosing interval). Our search identified three
ongoing studies that are investigating the safety and efectiveness

to follow up both women and children longer term so that
the full impact of diferent corticosteroids and regimens can be

Study characteristics
Methods
Randomised controlled trial
Participants
679 women with 763 fetuses assigned to receive dexamethasone and 667 women with 746 fetuses as-
signed to receive betamethasone 
Setting: 14 maternity hospitals, Australia and New Zealand
Inclusion criteria: women at risk of preterm birth < 34 weeks' gestation, with single or twin pregnancy
and no contraindication to corticosteroids
Exclusion criteria: women with chorioamnionitis that necessitated urgent delivery, already received
antenatal corticosteroids, in the second stage of labour or known fetal lung maturation
Interventions
Dexamethasone group (679 women, 763 fetuses)
Dexamethasone sodium phosphate 24 mg: 12 mg IM 24 hours apart
Betamethasone group (667 women, 746 fetuses) 
Betamethasone acetate/phosphate (Celestene chronadose) 22.8 mg: 11.4 mg IM 24 hours apart 
Repeat treatments (single dose of initial treatment) permitted following assessment at weekly intervals
Outcomes
Primary outcome
•
Death or neurosensory disability at 2 years of age
Secondary outcomes
•
At 2 years old: death or major neurosensory disability, blindness, deafness, cerebral palsy, develop-
mental delay, cognitive, language and motor score, body size at 2 years of age, use of health service
since discharge, blood pressure, Child Behaviour Checklist
•
Infant: IVH, PVL, ROP, PDA, RDS, chronic lung disease, mechanical ventilation, infection, NICU admis-
sion, body size at birth (weight, length, head circumference) and z scores, body size and z scores at
hospital discharge.
•
Maternal: infection-related morbidities (chorioamnionitis requiring intrapartum antibiotics, postna-
tal antibiotics), induction of labour, caesarean section (reasons for caesarean section), postpartum
haemorrhage, blood transfusion, postnatal length of stay (days).
Notes
Dates of study: January 2009 to February 2013
Funding source: National Health and Medical Research Council (Australia) 
Declarations of interest: no competing interests

Interventions
Dexamethasone group
Dexamethasone phosphate 4 × 6 mg 12-hourly regimen (starting immediately after randomisation
at time points 0 hours, 12 hours, 24 hours and 36 hours) or until birth occurs, whichever comes first.
If the full regimen is completed, the woman would have received a total of 24 mg of dexametha-
sone in divided doses
Betamethasone group
Betamethasone phosphate 4 × 2 mg IM 12-hourly regimen (starting immediately after randomisa-
tion at time points 0 hours, 12 hours, 24 hours and 36 hours) or until birth occurs, whichever comes
first. If the full regimen is completed, the woman would have received a total of betamethasone
phosphate 8 mg in divided doses
Control
Identical placebo, same regimen and dexamethasone and betamethasone groups, i.e. adminis-
tered every 12 hours, to a total of 4 doses (time points 0 hours, 12 hours, 24 hours and 36 hours) or
until birth occurs, whichever comes first.

hours with an FiO2 0.4 at any time, continuous use of supplementary oxygen for ≥ 24 hours with
an FiO2 0.4 at any time

D I F F E R E N C E S   B E T W E E N   P R O T O C O L   A N D   R E V I E W
Review title
For this 2022 update, in light of consumer feedback we have amend the review title. Previously the title was 'Diferent corticosteroids and
regimens for accelerating fetal lung maturation for women at risk of preterm birth', however it is babies rather than women that are at risk
of direct harm due to preterm birth and that corticosteroids stand to benefit.
Outcomes
For this 2022 update, we revised the primary mortality outcome for the baby to 'all known deaths afer randomisation'.
The outcome Intraventricular haemorrhage (IVH) was previously defined 'diagnosed by ultrasound, diagnosed by autopsy'. In line with
methods adopted by all trials conducted by the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth group, we have amended this definition to 'diagnosed
by ultrasound or diagnosed by autopsy', reflecting the fact that where studies diagnosed IVH only using autopsy (and not ultrasound), we
would not report their results. This did not apply to any of our included studies.
For this update, we removed results for outcomes that had not been prespecified: caesarean section; gestational age at birth; mean Apgar
score at five minutes and vasopressor use.
Our developmental delay and intellectual impairment secondary outcomes are defined in the protocol as developmental quotient less than
–2 standard deviations below population mean. For this 2022 update, we clarified that this constitutes moderate or severe delay, and we
have also included a broader developmental delay outcome encompassing all of mild, moderate and severe delay (developmental quotient
less than –1 standard deviations below population mean). This review update provided evidence for updating World Health Organization
recommendations on use of antenatal corticosteroids, and this broader outcome was needed for the guideline update.
In the 2013 update, the number of primary outcomes for the baby was reduced to three (death, respiratory distress syndrome and IVH)
and remaining outcomes were reclassified as secondary outcomes.
Prior to the 2013 update, the outcomes any neurodisability for the child, and for the child as an adult were added.
Unit of analysis issues
In this update of the review, we clarified that we excluded cross-over trials and cluster-randomised trials, and included studies reported
as abstracts only.
For this update, we clarified that "the unit of randomisation was per woman: for maternal outcomes, we used the number of women as
the denominator; where possible, for fetal and neonatal outcomes where some women had multiple pregnancies,  we used the number
of babies as the denominator", and revised previously included data where appropriate.

Dealing with missing data
For this update, we clarified in our methods what denominators were used, where data were missing from the original reports. Further
to the above,
"In the absence of appropriate statistical methods in the individual trials to account for missing data, in the following situations we deemed
it appropriate to use the denominator reported by the trial rather than the number randomised in order to avoid making  potentially
misleading assumptions about the outcomes for those women and fetuses with missing data:
•
where no explanation was given for women who were lost to follow-up before giving birth and were not included in the analysis of the
individual trials;
•
where women were not included in trial analysis because they were randomised in error (e.g. multiple pregnancy in a singleton
pregnancy-only trial);
•
where women or babies were not included in the trial analysis for outcomes recorded postdischarge (e.g. developmental outcomes at
two years)."
Subgroup analyses
For the 2022 update, because we believe that these characteristics may afect health outcomes, we planned to undertake additional
subgroup analyses by;
•
chorioamnionitis at trial entry;
•
fetal growth restriction at trial entry;
•
pregestational and gestational diabetes at trial entry.
For the 2013 update, a previously excluded subgroup (see below) was included in the review methods as it is possible that this maternal
characteristic may afect health outcomes:
•
preterm prelabour rupture of membranes (at trial entry: yes versus no).
Prior to the 2013 update, the following subgroup was deleted from the review methods, as it may be influenced by the intervention:
•
gestational age at birth (24 to 26 weeks, 27 to 29 weeks, 30 to 34 weeks, 35 to 37 weeks).
